items.question_text: A 58-year-old man has a positive faecal immunochemical test. He has read that the test is 70% sensitive and asks what his chance of cancer is. You cannot quote his personal chance from sensitivity alone. What is the most appropriate explanation?
options: His chance of cancer cannot be stated from sensitivity and specificity alone
His chance of cancer is 95%
Specificity of 90% means 90% of positive tests are true
A positive test in a sensitive assay means the disease is present
His chance of cancer is 90%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. His chance of cancer cannot be stated from sensitivity and specificity alone

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A 58-year-old man has a positive faecal immunochemical test. He has read that the test is 70% sensitive and asks what his chance of cancer is. You cannot quote his personal chance from sensitivity alone.

2. THE RULE
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Sensitivity is the proportion of people with disease who test positive. Specificity is the proportion without disease who test negative. Neither is the positive predictive value. PPV needs prevalence as well.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. His chance of cancer is 95%: That is the sensitivity, not his post-test probability.
C. Specificity of 90% means 90% of positive tests are true: That confuses specificity with PPV.
D. A positive test in a sensitive assay means the disease is present: A sensitive test still has false positives.
E. His chance of cancer is 90%: That is the specificity.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties; a negative highly sensitive test helps rule disease out, and the post-test probability also needs prevalence or likelihood ratios.

---

PPV is the same. The test characteristics are unchanged
PPV is higher where prevalence is higher
Sensitivity falls when prevalence falls
PPV is higher in the university clinic because the students are healthier
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. PPV is higher where prevalence is higher

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
The same test has a lower positive predictive value in the low-prevalence clinic.

2. THE RULE
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with fixed sensitivity and specificity it falls as prevalence falls, so most positives may be false in a low-prevalence population.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
PPV is true positives divided by all positives. At low prevalence most positives are false positives, so PPV falls. Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test. PPV is a property of the test in a population.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. PPV equals specificity in both clinics: They are different quantities.
B. PPV is the same. The test characteristics are unchanged: Sensitivity and specificity are unchanged. PPV is not.
D. Sensitivity falls when prevalence falls: Sensitivity does not.
E. PPV is higher in the university clinic because the students are healthier: Lower prevalence lowers PPV.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
PPV rises with prevalence.

---

items.question_text: A registrar confuses two figures in a report. One is the number of new cases of a disease in a year. The other is the number of people who currently have it. What is the most appropriate distinction?
options: Incidence includes deaths. Prevalence does not
Incidence counts existing cases. Prevalence counts new cases
Prevalence always falls when incidence is stable
They are interchangeable in chronic disease
Incidence is new cases in a period. Prevalence is existing cases at a time
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Incidence is new cases in a period. Prevalence is existing cases at a time

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Incidence is new cases. Prevalence is existing cases. A stable incidence can still raise prevalence.

2. THE RULE
Incidence is new cases in a population over a period of time, while prevalence is all existing cases at a point in time.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Incidence is the rate of new cases. Prevalence is the proportion who have the disease at a point. Prevalence can rise if people live longer with the disease, even when incidence is flat.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Incidence includes deaths. Prevalence does not: Deaths remove people from the prevalent pool.
B. Incidence counts existing cases. Prevalence counts new cases: That reverses the definitions.
C. Prevalence always falls when incidence is stable: Longer survival raises prevalence.
D. They are interchangeable in chronic disease: The distinction matters more in chronic disease, not less.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Incidence is new cases over time.

---

items.question_text: A trial reports that a treatment reduces the absolute risk of an outcome from 8% to 4%. A student asks for the number needed to treat. What is the number needed to treat?
options: NNT is 10
NNT is 4
NNT is 25
NNT cannot be calculated without the p-value
NNT is 40
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. NNT is 25

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Absolute reduction is 4 percentage points. NNT is 25, not 4.

2. THE RULE
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Absolute risk reduction is 10% minus 6%, which is 4 percentage points, or 0.04. NNT is 1 / 0.04 = 25. The 40% figure is the relative risk reduction and is not the NNT.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. NNT is 10: That is the placebo event rate, not the difference.
B. NNT is 4: That treats the relative reduction as if it were the absolute one.
D. NNT cannot be calculated without the p-value: NNT is an effect size. The p-value is a separate question.
E. NNT is 40: That is the relative reduction written as a whole number.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
NNT = 1 / absolute risk reduction.

---

The 50% is relative. The absolute reduction is 1 event per 1000 people.

The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Relative risk reduction is (2 − 1) / 2 = 50%. Absolute risk reduction is 1 per 1000. The advertisement uses the relative figure. The absolute figure is what tells the patient how many events are prevented.

A. The absolute reduction is 50%: 50% is the relative figure.
B. Half of vaccinated people avoid the outcome: That misreads a relative reduction as a personal probability.
C. Relative risk reduction cannot exceed absolute risk reduction: Relative often exceeds absolute when the baseline is small.
E. The trial shows no effect because the rates are both small: Small rates can still have a real relative effect.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Always pair a relative reduction with the absolute one.

items.question_text: A trial reports a relative risk of 0.8 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.5 to 1.3. A colleague says the treatment works because the point estimate is under 1. Statistical significance is not shown. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: The treatment is proven harmful
The interval includes 1, so a null effect is not excluded
A confidence interval is the range of individual patient results
The p-value must be below 0.05 because the point estimate moved
The result is statistically significant because 0.80 is below 1
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. The interval includes 1, so a null effect is not excluded

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
The interval crosses 1. The point estimate of 0.80 does not prove an effect.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value, here a relative risk of 1, does not exclude no effect. The point estimate of 0.80 is the best single guess. It is not proof.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The treatment is proven harmful: The interval also includes benefit.
C. A confidence interval is the range of individual patient results: It is an interval for the estimated effect, not for individual outcomes.
D. The p-value must be below 0.05 because the point estimate moved: An interval crossing 1 corresponds to a p-value above 0.05.
E. The result is statistically significant because 0.80 is below 1: Significance is about the interval or the p-value, not the direction of the point estimate alone.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
An interval that includes the null does not exclude no effect.

---

items.question_text: A paper reports p = 0.03 for a difference. A student says this means there is a 3% chance the result is due to chance, or a 97% chance the treatment works. What is the most appropriate explanation?

p = 0.03 means the drug works in 97% of patients
p = 0.03 is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null were true
p = 0.03 is the probability the null is true
A p-value below 0.05 means the study was adequately powered
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. p = 0.03 is the probability of a result at least this extreme if the null were true

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
p = 0.03 is not a 3% chance that the drug does not work.

2. THE RULE
A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
The p-value is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed, assuming the null is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it is not a measure of clinical importance.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. p = 0.03 proves the effect is clinically important: Statistical significance is not clinical importance.
B. p = 0.03 means the drug works in 97% of patients: That confuses a p-value with a response rate.
D. p = 0.03 is the probability the null is true: That is the common misreading.
E. A p-value below 0.05 means the study was adequately powered: Power is set before the study. A small p-value does not prove it.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A p-value assumes the null and describes the data.

items.question_text: A screening program reports longer survival from diagnosis in screened patients than in unscreened patients. A colleague says this proves the program reduces deaths. What is the most appropriate caution?

Screening always reduces mortality if survival from diagnosis rises
Lead time applies only to infectious disease
Longer survival from diagnosis proves a mortality benefit

CORRECT ANSWER

A. Earlier diagnosis can lengthen survival time without delaying death

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Longer survival from diagnosis is not proof of benefit. The diagnosis may simply have been made earlier.

2. THE RULE
Lead-time and length-time biases can make screening look beneficial for survival without delaying death.

3. WHY A IS CORRECT
Lead time is the interval between screen detection and the time the disease would have presented clinically. Survival measured from diagnosis lengthens by that interval even if the date of death is unchanged.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
B. This is length-time bias: Length-time bias is the tendency of screening to find slower-growing disease.
C. Screening always reduces mortality if survival from diagnosis rises: That is the biased reading.
D. Lead time applies only to infectious disease: It is a screening concept.
E. Longer survival from diagnosis proves a mortality benefit: The clock started earlier.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Lead-time bias shifts the start of the survival clock.

---

items.question_text: In a randomised trial, some patients allocated to treatment did not take it, and some allocated to control obtained it elsewhere. A student wants to analyse only those who took the treatment. It preserves the randomisation. What is the most appropriate analysis?
options: Analyse only those who received the allocated treatment. That measures efficacy
Intention to treat applies only to drug trials
Analyse by allocated group. That is the intention-to-treat estimate
Move the crossovers into the arm they ended up in
Exclude anyone who missed a visit
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Analyse by allocated group. That is the intention-to-treat estimate

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Keep people in the arm they were randomised to. Dropping crossovers breaks the protection of randomisation.

2. THE RULE
Intention-to-treat analysis keeps participants in their allocated group, and allocation concealment differs from blinding.

3. WHY C IS CORRECT
Intention to treat keeps every randomised participant in the allocated arm. It estimates the effect of offering the treatment, preserves randomisation, and avoids bias from drop-out and crossover. A per-protocol analysis answers a different question and can mislead.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. Analyse only those who received the allocated treatment. That measures efficacy: That is per-protocol. It is not the primary unbiased estimate.
B. Intention to treat applies only to drug trials: It applies to any randomised comparison.
D. Move the crossovers into the arm they ended up in: That is as-treated analysis and breaks randomisation.
E. Exclude anyone who missed a visit: Missingness is handled. It is not a reason to drop the principle.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Intention to treat follows allocation, not receipt.

---

It is a cross-sectional prevalence survey of solariums

items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. It is a case-control study and estimates an odds ratio, not an incidence

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
This is a case-control study. It does not measure how many solarium users developed melanoma that year.

2. THE RULE
Study design determines what can be estimated: case-control studies give odds ratios, cohorts give incidence, and cross-sectional studies cannot show temporal direction.

3. WHY B IS CORRECT
Cases and controls are sampled on disease status, then exposures are compared. The usual estimate is an odds ratio. Incidence cannot be read off unless the study is nested in a defined cohort.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. It is a randomised trial: Nothing was assigned.
C. It is a cross-sectional prevalence survey of solariums: Cross-sectional samples a population at one time, not cases and controls.
D. It can calculate a 1-year risk directly: The sampling was on disease, so the risk in users is not observed.
E. It is a cohort study and estimates incidence: A cohort starts with exposure, not with disease.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Case-control samples on disease.

---

B. A common outcome makes the odds ratio smaller than the relative risk: It makes it larger.

Relative risk is the risk ratio.

A 95% confidence interval that includes the null value is compatible with no effect, and a non-significant result in a small study may be a type II error.

E. Type I error is the failure to detect a real effect: That is type II.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
Type II error is missing a real effect.

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A newspaper reports that a new drug halves the risk of stroke. In the trial, the stroke rate fell from 2 per 1000 to 1 per 1000 over 5 years. A patient asks what this means for him.

The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

B. No benefit occurred: There was a small absolute benefit.
C. Half of people are saved: Only 1 in 1000 avoids the event.
D. Relative and absolute reductions are the same: A 50% relative reduction equals only a 0.1% absolute reduction here.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
The number needed to treat is 1 divided by the absolute risk reduction, and relative risk reductions overstate small absolute benefits.

items.question_text: Coffee drinkers have more heart disease and also smoke more. The smoking difference could explain the finding. Causation is not shown. Which of the following is most accurate?
options: The coffee association is therefore causal
No confounder can be associated with both
Adjustment is unnecessary
Smoking may confound the coffee association
Randomisation has occurred
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Smoking may confound the coffee association

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
Coffee drinkers have more heart disease and also smoke more. The smoking difference could explain the finding. Causation is not shown.

2. THE RULE
A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the association, and unmeasured confounders can persist after adjustment.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
A confounder is associated with the exposure and the outcome. Smoking fits.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. The coffee association is therefore causal: Confounding by smoking may explain the association.
B. No confounder can be associated with both: A confounder is by definition associated with both.
C. Adjustment is unnecessary: Adjustment or stratification for smoking is needed.
E. Randomisation has occurred: This is an observational association; there was no randomisation.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
A confounder is linked to both exposure and outcome and distorts the association, and unmeasured confounders can persist after adjustment.

---

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
In a cohort the outcome is 20% in the exposed and 10% in the unexposed. The relative risk is 2.

2. THE RULE
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

3. WHY E IS CORRECT
Common outcome. RR is 2. OR is higher. Report the relative risk.

A. The odds ratio is the relative risk: With a common outcome the OR (2.25) exceeds the RR (2).
B. RR is 2.25: RR is 0.20/0.10 = 2; 2.25 is the odds ratio.
C. Risk cannot be calculated in a cohort: Cohorts measure risk directly.
D. OR and RR are identical when the outcome is common: OR and RR diverge when the outcome is common.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

---

When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

Common outcome inflates the odds ratio relative to the risk ratio.

E. The odds ratio is always smaller than the relative risk: For a harmful exposure the OR is further from 1, not smaller.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
When the outcome is common, the odds ratio overstates the relative risk, so cohort data should report the relative risk.

items.question_text: A screening test has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 95%. It is offered to an asymptomatic population in which the prevalence of the disease is 1%. A man in this population has a positive result and asks how likely it is that he has the disease. What is the closest estimate?
options: About 15%
items.explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. About 15%

---

1. CLINICAL SITUATION
A positive screening result is being interpreted in a low-prevalence population.

2. THE RULE
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence: with fixed sensitivity and specificity it falls as prevalence falls, so most positives may be false in a low-prevalence population.

3. WHY D IS CORRECT
Per 10,000 people: 100 have the disease and 90 test positive (true positives). 9,900 do not, and 5% of them, 495, test positive (false positives). PPV = 90 / (90 + 495), about 15%. When prevalence is low, false positives outnumber true positives even with a good test, so a positive screen needs diagnostic confirmation.

4. WHY THE OTHER OPTIONS ARE WRONG
A. 1%: 1% is the pre-test prevalence. A positive result raises the probability to about 15%.
B. 90%: 90% is the sensitivity, P(positive given disease). It is not P(disease given positive).
C. 50%: 50% would need far higher prevalence or specificity than this.
E. 95%: 95% is the specificity, which concerns people without the disease.

5. KEY TAKEAWAY
At low prevalence, PPV falls sharply: here about 15% despite 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity.

---
